title: No-conduction-path rule: NEMS relay as the cell access switch
idea: Self-imposed limit: the off state may contain no solid conduction path at all. Replace the access MOSFET with a vertical nano-electromechanical relay sitting on the capacitor: a 10 nm gap with a low-adhesion Ru- or Pt-coated contact that the wordline pulls in electrostatically. When open, the vacuum/air gap leaks less than an attoamp, so retention is set only by capacitor dielectric leakage.
why: Fact 3: removes the <=13 fA subthreshold, GIDL and junction tail entirely. Refresh goes from 64 ms to minutes or hours, and the 16-33% idle refresh power nearly vanishes. Risk: contact endurance (~1e15 cycles needed) and ns switching at nanoscale.

title: Wordline-swing ceiling of 1 V: band-to-band tunnel FET access device
idea: Limit: the access device may swing only 1 V yet must still cut off by 10 decades. Use a vertical p-i-n tunnel FET (SiGe source pocket, Si channel, n+ storage-side drain). It turns on by band-to-band tunneling at sub-60 mV/dec and has no thermionic subthreshold tail, so off-current is set by the reverse-biased p-i-n diode (aA range). Asymmetric doping blocks ambipolar leakage from the storage side.
why: Facts 3 and 10: lets VPP drop from 3 V toward ~1.5 V (~4x less wordline CV2) and removes the thermionic tail that forces refresh. A low on-current (~1 uA) still charges 5 fF in under 10 ns.

title: Wordlines capped at VARY: negative-capacitance HZO gate amplifies switching
idea: Limit: no wordline may exceed the array voltage. Add a 5 nm Zr-rich HZO negative-capacitance layer to the access transistor gate stack, capacitance-matched to the channel so internal voltage amplification gives ~40 mV/dec hysteresis-free switching. The same Ion/Ioff then needs ~1 V less swing, or the same swing gives ~25x lower leakage.
why: Facts 3, 7 and 10: retires the boosted 3 V wordline and its charge pumps (periphery area), or lengthens retention ~10x. Unlike prior HZO memory work, the ferroelectric is a gain element inside the switch, not the storage.

title: Ban all implants: fixed-charge dielectrics electrostatically dope the access transistor
idea: Limit: no dopant atom may be implanted near the storage node. Fixed charge in the spacer dielectric induces the source/drain extensions instead: positive-charge SiNx for n-type, negative-charge Al2O3 for p-type. The result is an atomically abrupt, damage-free 'junction' with no random dopant fluctuation and no end-of-range defects to act as SRH generation centers.
why: Fact 3: implant damage and dopant clusters seed the high-leakage tail. Removing them could pull worst-cell leakage from ~13 fA toward the median, ~10x, and the refresh interval would stretch accordingly.

title: Storage node may touch no pn junction: MIS tunnel contact
idea: Limit: the storage node may not have a depletion junction to the substrate. Contact the capacitor through a ~1 nm Al2O3/SiO2 interlayer onto a fully depleted ultrathin-body channel. This metal-insulator-semiconductor contact passes write current by direct tunneling and eliminates the junction depletion volume, where SRH thermal generation and trap-assisted tunneling create the tail.
why: Fact 3: junction leakage is a dominant tail component. With no junction volume, worst-cell generation falls ~10-100x and refresh could stretch toward ~1 s.

title: Only 10 nm may change: wide-gap Si:C pocket against GIDL
idea: Limit: the channel stays silicon, and only the 10 nm under the gate-drain overlap may be altered. Selectively grow a carbon-alloyed Si1-yCy or 3C-SiC pocket at the storage-side drain edge. Its wider local bandgap exponentially suppresses band-to-band GIDL tunneling where the negative wordline meets the high storage node.
why: Facts 3 and 10: BTBT current scales roughly as exp(-Eg^1.5/F). Widening the local gap by 0.2-0.3 eV could cut GIDL ~10-30x and allow a deeper negative off-voltage without a GIDL penalty.

title: Intrinsic carriers below one per chip: amorphous Ga2O3 access channel
idea: Limit: the channel's intrinsic carrier density must make thermal leakage physically negligible. Use ALD amorphous Ga2O3 (Eg ~4.8 eV, no indium) as a BEOL access-transistor channel, with source/drain doped by oxygen vacancies from a local H2 plasma. The theoretical off-current floor is ~1e-24 A/um, orders of magnitude below IGZO.
why: Fact 3 and resources: refresh-free retention of hours or more at 85 C, no exposure to indium supply concentration, and the device stacks in BEOL for 3D tiers (fact 2). Risk: mobility below 5 cm2/Vs demands a short channel.

title: Delete the electrical wordline: optically gated photoconductive access switch
idea: Limit: no metal wordline is allowed over the array. Each cell's access device is a wide-gap GaN or ZnO photoconductor bridge between the bitline and the storage node. A row is 'opened' by a light pulse through a SiN waveguide with grating taps, fed by edge micro-LEDs or lasers. In the dark the bridge holds almost no carriers.
why: Facts 3, 9 and 10: dark leakage of ~aA nearly eliminates refresh. With no wordlines there is no row-hammer coupling and no 3 V wordline CV2 energy. Risks: photoconductor speed (<1 ns needed) and persistent photoconductivity.

title: No carriers in the off-state: vacuum-channel field-emission access device
idea: Limit: the off-state medium must contain no carriers. Build a sealed 20 nm vacuum nanogap between a sharp emitter tip on the storage node and a bitline collector, with a surrounding gate as the wordline. The device turns on only by field emission above a threshold field; below it, Fowler-Nordheim current falls super-exponentially.
why: Fact 3: near-zero off-current makes refresh rare. Field emission is temperature-insensitive, which also removes the hot-temperature doubling of refresh. Speculative because of vacuum sealing and emitter wear.

title: Charging-energy wall: Coulomb-blockade island as the leakage stopper
idea: Limit: leakage must be stopped by a quantum effect, not a barrier height. Put a sub-2 nm silicon or metal nanocrystal island in series with the access channel. Its charging energy (>0.5 eV) blocks single-electron transit until the wordline shifts the island level into resonance, and co-tunneling leakage is exponentially suppressed.
why: Fact 3: the off-state is set by the charging energy (~20 kT), not by doping or trap statistics, which could collapse the tail distribution. Speculative: island uniformity at room temperature.

title: Zero refresh energy from the supply: Esaki tunnel-diode latch storage node
idea: Limit: holding data may cost no refresh cycles at all. Hang a pair of series Esaki tunnel diodes from each storage node to a standby rail. Their negative-differential-resistance load line gives two stable node voltages. Picoamp tunnel current continuously compensates leakage, so the cell latches like static memory in a DRAM footprint.
why: Fact 3: turns ~46 fJ/bit of refresh energy into a static picoamp hold current and frees the 10-20% of bandwidth refresh consumes. Risks: diode peak-to-valley ratio at nm scale and standby current density.

title: Refresh commands rationed to zero: per-row canary cells call refresh
idea: Limit: the controller may issue no periodic refresh. Each row carries 2 deliberately weakened replica cells (thinner capacitor, longer drain overlap) that always hold '1' and feed a tiny comparator on the local sense line. When a canary decays past threshold, the row raises a flag and is restored. Refresh becomes event-driven and tracks real temperature and VRT.
why: Fact 3: most rows retain data for seconds, so restoring only when a canary trips could cut refresh operations ~10-50x versus 64 ms worst-case scheduling and removes temperature guardbands.

title: Refresh may consume no fresh charge: adiabatic bitline recycling between subarrays
idea: Limit: every refresh must reuse the charge of the previous one. Pair subarrays through transfer switches. After subarray A restores, its full-swing bitlines step their charge adiabatically into subarray B's bitlines, which are being precharged, instead of dumping it to ground. This charge seesaw leaves the sense amps only the difference to top up.
why: Fact 3: bitline swing dominates refresh energy. Recycling ~50-60% of it cuts refresh from ~46 fJ/bit toward ~20 fJ/bit with no change to the cell.

title: Bias-only toolbox: co-pulse plate and well during idle
idea: Limit: no process change; only array biases may move. In long idle or self-refresh, ramp the cell plate and the array p-well down together by ~0.3-0.5 V. Every storage node then level-shifts down capacitively without forward-biasing its junction, which shrinks both the storage-to-wordline voltage that drives GIDL and the Vds of '1' cells. Both rails return before activation.
why: Facts 3 and 10: GIDL and junction leakage are exponential in field, so a 0.4 V shift could cut standby tail leakage ~5-10x. Standby is where refresh takes 16-33% of idle power.

title: Check bits capped at 3%: Z-channel codes for one-way leakage
idea: Limit: no more ECC overhead than today. Retention errors are unidirectional: charged cells decay, empty cells do not, and polarity is fixed per true or anti cell. Map logical bits to physical polarity, then encode each 512-bit row segment with asymmetric (Z-channel, Varshamov-Tenengolts-style) codes. These correct t one-way errors with far fewer check bits than symmetric BCH.
why: Fact 3: correcting ~2-3x more retention errors at equal overhead permits ~4-8x longer refresh intervals in the exponential-tail regime, a direct cut to refresh energy and bandwidth loss.

title: Refresh fixed at one second: sense amps flag low-confidence bits
idea: Limit: the refresh interval is forced to 1 s and the cell cannot improve. Add a dual-reference margin check to the sense amp (a second sense against a shifted reference) so cells whose signal sits near the decision point are flagged as erasures. The ECC decoder can then correct about twice as many errors, because an erasure costs half a correction.
why: Fact 3: knowing where the weak bits are doubles effective correction power, making 1 s refresh tolerable and cutting refresh energy and bandwidth ~15x.

title: Tail removal allowed only after packaging: wordline Joule self-anneal
idea: Limit: the leakage tail must be fixed in the field, not in the fab. In maintenance windows, drive a controlled current through segmented wordline straps to Joule-heat a few-um2 region to ~300 C for microseconds. This anneals variable-retention-time trap configurations and redistributes hydrogen at the access transistor's Si/SiO2 interface; the weak rows are then re-profiled.
why: Fact 3: VRT traps drive the 13 fA tail and its unpredictability. Periodic in-situ annealing could shrink the tail ~3-10x over life and allow longer refresh. Risk: thermal stress on neighboring cells.

title: Leakage must be a product, not a sum: stacked double-gate pillar
idea: Limit: no single gate may hold off the full voltage. In a vertical-channel 4F2 pillar, split the gate into two stacked electrodes that are driven together to turn on. When off, the mid-channel node floats to an intermediate potential, so each segment sees about half the Vds, and DIBL and GIDL drop superlinearly (the stack effect) at zero added footprint.
why: Fact 3: the stack effect cuts off-current ~10x in logic. In a vertical cell the second gate costs height, not area, so the refresh interval could rise ~5-10x.

title: Metal impurities rationed to zero: carbon-cluster proximity gettering under storage junctions
idea: Limit: no transition-metal atom may survive within 1 um of a storage junction. Implant carbon-cluster (C3H5) ions to form a gettering layer a few hundred nm beneath the array, the trick CMOS image sensors use against hot pixels. The layer captures Fe, Ni and Cu that would otherwise sit in junction depletion regions as deep-level generation centers.
why: Fact 3: the extreme leakage tail is tied to deep-level metal contaminants. Image sensors cut white-pixel counts ~10x this way; a similar tail compression would allow 2-4x longer refresh.

title: Thresholds must move only twice per idle: ferroelectric Vt-parking access transistor
idea: Limit: leakage may be killed only by a stored state, not by continuous bias. Embed a thin HZO layer in the access gate stack. Before a long idle, one global pulse polarizes it so every access transistor's Vt rises ~0.5 V ('parked', ~1e8 lower subthreshold leakage); an un-park pulse restores the low Vt before access. Ferroelectric endurance is spent only on rare idle transitions.
why: Fact 3: self-refresh dominates idle power. Parked arrays could hold data for minutes between refreshes, a 100x+ cut in standby refresh energy. This is distinct from using HZO as the storage element.

title: Data that dies young gets no refresh: lifetime-tagged no-refresh banks
idea: Limit: refresh only bits that will outlive the retention window. The runtime tags allocations with a time-to-live and places short-lived ones (activations, attention scratch, gradient buffers overwritten every few ms) in banks with refresh disabled. A hardware lease timer raises an error if any data is read after its window.
why: Fact 3: a large share of AI training and inference DRAM traffic is short-lived. Taking those banks out of refresh recovers their share of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth and of idle power.

title: Borrow the image sensor's darkness: pinned storage diode with transfer gate
idea: Limit: the storage node may never touch an oxide interface. Store the bit as electrons in a buried n-well under a p+ pinning layer, as in a 4T CMOS image-sensor pixel, and write and read it through a transfer gate to a floating-diffusion sense node with a gain transistor. Pinning eliminates interface-state generation, which is how image sensors reach dark currents of ~1e-18 A per pixel.
why: Fact 3: dark currents 1000x below the DRAM tail push retention to minutes or hours, and gain readout reduces the charge needed (fact 1). Costs: gain-cell-class area and full-transfer speed.

title: Idle power budget of 1 mW per GB: in-DRAM compaction before self-refresh
idea: Limit: in self-refresh the die may refresh only the rows it truly needs. On self-refresh entry, an on-die engine applies zero, pattern and base-delta compression to each subarray, packs the data into fewer subarrays with in-DRAM row copy, and stops refreshing the vacated subarrays. It decompresses on exit.
why: Fact 3: AI and server data compress ~2-3x, so self-refresh energy falls ~50-65% for idle devices.

title: No fab, only an FPGA: per-row refresh via ACT/PRE
idea: 10-person constraint: we cannot touch the die, so we own the controller. An FPGA CXL memory expander profiles every row of commodity DDR5 at boot. It then replaces blanket auto-refresh with targeted ACT->PRE restores scheduled per row from a retention table: 64 ms for the weakest ~0.1%, 1-4 s for the rest, plus a VRT guardband.
why: Fact 3: 90%+ of refresh operations are spent on strong rows. This recovers most of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth and cuts refresh energy ~5-10x on unmodified DRAM, using only an FPGA board, firmware and a CXL IP license.

title: Controller-only polarity steering: weak cells always store their discharged state
idea: 10-person constraint: with no process access, we exploit what we can learn about the cells. After profiling each row's true/anti-cell layout and weak cells, the controller picks one of a few per-row XOR masks (kept in a side table) so the row's weak cells always hold their discharged, non-leaking value. Rows whose weak cells are all parked empty drop to the slow refresh tier.
why: Fact 3: weak cells fail only when charged. Steering them to the empty state removes them from the refresh-setting tail and moves ~80%+ of weak rows to an interval of 1 s or more.

title: Ten people, one kernel module: retire weak pages, run 4x tREFI
idea: 10-person constraint: ship software plus a BIOS setting. A kernel module runs a retention test at 4x the refresh interval and retires the ~0.01-0.1% of 4 KB pages that fail (BadRAM-style memmap exclusion). It stores the compressed failing-page list in the DIMM's user-writable SPD bytes so the list travels with the module, then sets tREFI 4x longer.
why: Fact 3: cuts refresh energy ~75% and recovers ~8-15% of bandwidth for under 0.1% of capacity, on any server, with no new hardware.

title: Buy the rejects: harvest downbinned DRAM with remap firmware
idea: 10-person constraint: we cannot make bits, so we rescue them. Buy retention-failing or downbinned DRAM dies, plus decommissioned hyperscaler DIMMs that fail the 64 ms/85 C screen, at scrap prices. Re-grade them on an FPGA tester and sell them on CXL cards whose controller combines weak-row remap, extra refresh for only the weak rows, and spare capacity.
why: Scarce-resource and cost axes: a few percent of global output that is now scrapped or downbinned becomes usable supply at under 30% of contract price, with no fab.

title: Closed-loop refresh servo from DDR5 error-check-and-scrub counters
idea: 10-person constraint: no silicon, only firmware listening to the die. Read DDR5's built-in ECS (error check and scrub) counts and the on-die ECC error reports per bank. A PI controller stretches each bank's refresh interval until the corrected-error rate reaches a set target (e.g. 1e-12 per bit-hour), and backs off as temperature rises.
why: Fact 3: refresh follows actual leakage instead of the worst-case datasheet, typically 2-4x fewer refreshes at the same reliability. It ships as BMC or memory-controller firmware.

title: Use the dormant knob: PASR plus nightly memory compaction
idea: 10-person constraint: no new silicon, so use what LPDDR already ships. An OS patch compacts movable pages out of whole LPDDR5X segments when load is low, then sets the mode-register partial-array self-refresh (PASR) bits so the empty segments stop refreshing. A watermark policy re-enables them before they are allocated.
why: Fact 3: idle servers and phones often hold 30-60% free memory, and self-refresh energy falls in proportion when it stops being refreshed. It is a kernel patch a small team can upstream.

title: Refresh hides in compute bubbles: pull-in synchronized to AI kernel phases
idea: 10-person constraint: only the scheduler is ours. A runtime hook signals the memory controller when a compute-bound phase starts (e.g. a high-arithmetic-intensity GEMM tile). The controller pulls in up to the JEDEC-allowed 8 pending refreshes during that bubble and postpones refresh during bandwidth-bound phases.
why: Fact 3: refresh's 10-20% bandwidth tax moves into windows when DRAM bandwidth would sit idle, recovering most of it for memory-bound kernels via driver and firmware.

title: Let the model refresh itself: compiler sweeps every weight row per window
idea: 10-person constraint: a compiler pass instead of hardware. For inference, place and stream the weights so every DRAM row holding weights is activated at least once per 32 ms; each read restores its row. The controller disables explicit refresh for those banks and falls back to REF only if a token stall exceeds the window.
why: Fact 3: weights are the majority of inference DRAM bytes, so their refresh energy and bandwidth drop to ~zero with only a compiler change and a controller flag.

title: Recompute instead of refresh: checksummed recomputable activations
idea: 10-person constraint: a software library. Mark tensors that are cheap to recompute (activations saved for the backward pass, KV-cache prefixes) as recompute-on-loss and store them in relaxed-refresh regions (e.g. 1 s), with a 32-bit checksum per tile. On a mismatch, recompute the tile from its checkpointed inputs instead of paying refresh to protect it.
why: Fact 3: trades rare recomputation (<0.1% of FLOPs) for near-zero refresh on a large share of training memory.

title: BF16 split across refresh tiers: sign and exponent guarded, mantissa relaxed
idea: 10-person constraint: only data layout is ours. A custom allocator puts the sign-and-exponent byte planes of BF16/FP8 tensors in normally refreshed rows and the low mantissa bit-planes in rows refreshed every 1-2 s. It accepts rare low-order flips, which training and inference tolerate.
why: Fact 3: about half of tensor bits move to a ~20x slower refresh tier, cutting refresh energy ~45% for model memory with only an allocator and controller configuration.

title: Rent a furnace: high-pressure deuterium anneal of purchased DRAM wafers
idea: 10-person constraint: one tool, no fab. Buy known-good DRAM wafers before dicing and run a high-pressure (10-20 atm) deuterium anneal at 350-400 C, which drives D through the BEOL stack to passivate residual Si/SiO2 dangling bonds at the access transistors. Re-sort the results into long-retention bins and sell them as low-refresh parts.
why: Fact 3: high-pressure anneal studies show large interface-trap reductions, which could compress the leakage tail ~2-5x. A 10-person shop with one HP anneal tool creates a premium grade. Risk: BEOL thermal budget.

title: Thin the die, bias its back: backside retention-bias retrofit
idea: 10-person constraint: post-process purchased dies rather than run a fab. Thin commodity DRAM dies to ~20 um, deposit a backside contact, and add a package bond that applies negative substrate bias in standby. In processes where the array well couples to the substrate, the body effect raises access-transistor Vt and lowers standby leakage.
why: Fact 3: a 200-300 mV Vt rise gives ~10-100x less subthreshold leakage and far fewer self-refreshes. Risk: triple-well isolation may block the coupling, so each vendor's part needs a teardown first.

title: University cleanroom only: indium-free ALD zinc-tin-oxide access TFTs on MPW CMOS
idea: 10-person constraint: no fab, only a shared university cleanroom. Buy periphery-only CMOS wafers from a 130/180 nm MPW shuttle and post-process the BEOL at <=350 C: ALD ZnSnO channels (no indium or other scarce elements), ALD Al2O3 gates and planar MIM capacitors. This gives access devices with ~1e-20 A/um-class off-current stacked over the logic.
why: Facts 3 and 4 plus resources: demonstrates a refresh-free BEOL memory tile (hours of retention) with no EUV, no indium and no DRAM fab, buildable by ~10 people in ~18 months for niche low-density parts and as a pilot route.

title: Foundry SONOS as a trim knob: per-cell one-time Vt tuning
idea: 10-person constraint: only foundry-standard options are available to us. Design an eDRAM macro on a mature MPW process that offers SONOS charge-trap transistors, and use the SONOS device itself as the access transistor. At test, measure each cell's leakage and give leaky cells a single program pulse that raises their Vt 0.3-0.5 V for life, deleting the tail cell by cell.
why: Fact 3: the refresh interval is set by the worst cell. Trimming the tail to the median could lengthen refresh ~10x using standard foundry eNVM devices and a test program.

title: PMIC firmware only: undervolt DRAM rails during self-refresh to measured margin
idea: 10-person constraint: we can design only the DIMM's power path. DDR5 DIMMs carry their own PMIC, so custom PMIC firmware or a custom board steps VDD and VPP down during self-refresh to each module's minimum, found by a boot-time margin sweep, plus a 50 mV guard. Rails return to nominal on exit.
why: Facts 3 and 10: refresh energy scales roughly as V2, so 10-15% lower rails cut self-refresh energy ~20-28% per DIMM with board and firmware work only.

title: Thousand tiny tapeouts: crowdsourced access-device leakage variants on open PDKs
idea: 10-person constraint: crowdsource the search a small team cannot fund. Publish an open eDRAM access-device test-cell template for open-PDK shuttles (SKY130, GF180, IHP SG13G2). Pay bounties to hobbyists and students whose variants (gate shapes, well-bias tricks, guard rings, stacked devices) beat the baseline in silicon-measured retention, ranked by an automated FPGA tester.
why: Fact 3: hundreds of cheap parallel experiments explore leakage geometry faster than one team could, and the winners feed tail-reduction techniques into licensable IP.

title: Timing knobs only: extended restore time for weak rows
idea: 10-person constraint: only controller timing registers. Weak rows often fail because tight tRAS/tWR truncates their restore and leaves them at ~85-90% charge. The controller flags weak rows from profiling and gives only those activations and writes an extra 5-10 ns of restore, so the cell charges fully and its retention clears the slow-refresh threshold.
why: Fact 3: 10-20% more stored charge raises weak-row retention ~1.5-2x, which lets the global refresh tier relax a notch at under 0.1% performance cost.

title: Metadata replaces refresh: zero-row skip in the memory controller
idea: 10-person constraint: controller logic only. Keep a 1-bit-per-row all-zero bitmap, set by zeroing writes, OS page frees or detected zero rows. Rows marked zero leave the targeted-refresh schedule, and reads to them return zeros from the controller without activating the DRAM.
why: Fact 3: sparse tensors, padding and freshly zeroed pages often leave 10-30% of rows all-zero, and those rows stop costing refresh and activation energy.

title: Certify, don't fabricate: an R4 retention-grade standard and test lab
idea: 10-person constraint: create a market signal instead of a device. Define an open 'R4' grade (passes 256 ms at 85 C with ECC, VRT-screened over 3 thermal cycles) and run a small certification lab with FPGA testers. Hyperscalers and BIOS vendors auto-enable 4x tREFI for R4-labelled modules, so suppliers compete on their retention tail.
why: Fact 3: creates commercial pull for tail reduction and unlocks ~75% refresh savings fleet-wide through policy and a 10-person lab.

title: Shake out the liars: VRT provocation profiling with thermal and voltage cycling
idea: 10-person constraint: make cheap profiling trustworthy. Before any relaxed-refresh deployment, run a 6-hour provocation routine on the FPGA tester: 25-95 C thermal cycling (chamber or heat gun), VPP/VDD corners and worst-case neighbor data patterns. This makes variable-retention-time cells toggle into their leaky state so they get caught.
why: Fact 3: VRT is the reason profile-based refresh is unsafe. Catching 99%+ of VRT cells makes 4-16x refresh relaxation safe, and the test recipe is something a small lab can sell.

title: Compression pays for ECC: freed bits buy stronger codes
idea: 10-person constraint: controller logic only. Compress each 64 B line (base-delta or FP-exponent compression). When a line shrinks by at least 12.5%, store a stronger BCH or Reed-Solomon code in-line in the freed bits so the line can sit in a 4-8x slower refresh tier. Incompressible lines keep normal refresh.
why: Fact 3: with ~60-70% of AI and server lines compressible, most memory moves to a slow refresh tier at no capacity cost.

title: A patch table on the FPGA: weak bits live in SRAM
idea: 10-person constraint: no die changes. The CXL controller keeps a small CAM/SRAM table (~1 MB per 64 GB) with the address and correct value of every profiled weak bit. Reads are patched on the fly and writes update the table, so the DRAM runs at a refresh interval set by its strong-cell population.
why: Fact 3: the ~0.001% of weak bits stop setting refresh, which can move from 64 ms to over 1 s, at a cost of ~1 MB of SRAM per 64 GB.

title: Use the spare rows already inside: host-driven PPR for weak rows
idea: 10-person constraint: only JEDEC commands. DDR5 exposes host-initiated soft and hard post-package repair. Firmware runs the retention profile, then uses hPPR to fuse the worst row in each bank onto the die's own spare rows (and sPPR for temporary fixes), so the weakest rows physically leave the array before refresh is relaxed.
why: Fact 3: one worst row often sets each bank's refresh interval. Removing it raises the bank minimum by ~1.5-2x with firmware alone.
